newsitem.title: USA: US June CPI offers yet another benign price signal.
newsitem.headline: US June CPI offers yet another benign price signal.

text.p: U.S. consumer prices rose only negligibly in June, pointing to a reassuringly benign inflation environment and validating recent decisions by the Federal Reserve to hold interest rates steady, experts said.

Continuing to confound inflation hawks, who for some time have expected robust growth to filter through to higher inflation, consumer prices rose only 0.1 percent in both the overall and core readings, the Labor Department reported on Tuesday.
Wall Street economists had expected modest, albeit stronger, gains of 0.2 percent in the report's key components.
"The data is similar to the numbers we've seen in the last several months which show that inflation is still very benign," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
"What the numbers today do is verify that the Federal Reserve was correct in holding policy steady."
After pushing the federal funds rate up by 25 basis points for the first time in two years in late March, the Fed resisted further action in May and July.

Economists said that subdued energy prices, which were unchanged in June after a 2.4 percent decline in May, falling gold prices, unrecognized productivity gains and a strong dollar have all contributed to the confoundingly benign inflation backdrop.

In the June report, gasoline prices continued their steep decline, falling 0.9 percent after a whopping 4.1 percent drop-off in May. Home fuel oil, new car, and apparel prices also fell during the month.

The Labor Department said that the core consumer price reading, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose at a 2.4 percent seasonally adjusted annual rate during the first six months of the year -- the slowest pace since a 1.2 percent rise in the first half of 1965.
"There is every reason to think this year's core rate of inflation will be off a little bit from last year," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
"My guess is that the core is going to surprise us a little further.

A recent pause in average hourly earnings gains has assuaged concerns that rising wages might spark inflation down the road. And in the wake of Wednesday's price report, economists could see few additional reasons to worry about the price trend.
Thayer said he was keeping his eye on energy prices, which until now, have been critical in keeping inflation contained.

"We have seen energy prices stabilize at low levels in recent months, but if we do see a rebound in the latter half of the year the inflation environment might not look as favorable as it does today."
But economists conceded that worrying about a future pickup in inflation in the seventh year of an expansion was a luxury to be savored.
"I think what this is telling us is that there's almost a complete lack of inflationary pressures in the economy," said Cheryl Katz, a senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.
